text: Hi, I'm Elmor. This is a tour of the architecture behind Orders Shop: a dot net ten API, an ASP.NET Core backend for frontend, and a React single page app. I built it with AI assisted development, and I'll show you how the decisions, the tests, and the reviews keep that speed safe.
Here is the whole system. The browser talks to exactly one server, the BFF. All it holds is an HttpOnly cookie.
The BFF keeps the session in Valkey, and forwards allow listed calls to the Orders API. The API owns the business rules, and talks to PostgreSQL.
The whole stack starts with one docker compose command. And the API did not change when the front end was added.
Before any code, there is a plan. Requirements, a threat model, and fifteen architecture decision records. Each one compares options, and writes down why one won.

The AI writes code quickly, so the guardrails are strict. Architecture tests. Banned APIs that fail the build. And a fresh context review by separate reviewer agents, before anything merges. The decisions are mine and the product owner's. The AI does the typing.
The API uses Clean Architecture for the projects, and vertical slices for the folders. Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and one API project, which is the only composition root.
Inside each project, the first folder is the business feature: Products, Customers, Orders. Features never reference each other, and architecture tests fail the build if a layer rule is broken.
A request enters a thin FastEndpoints endpoint. Look at this one. A route, an explicit auth policy, an OpenAPI summary, and one line that sends a command.

The handler depends only on a messaging package, never on the web framework. It returns a Result, and one extension maps that to HTTP, with ProblemDetails for errors. Reads skip the bus, and use E F Core projections or Dapper.
PostgreSQL eighteen is the single database. E F Core handles every write and every migration. Dapper handles the views and report functions, where hand written SQL beats LINQ.

Rows are never deleted. Soft delete is enforced by an interceptor, and by the database itself, because the application role has no DELETE privilege. An audit interceptor writes the audit row in the same transaction, and never stores personal data values.

Concurrency is explicit. Entity tags come from the PostgreSQL xmin column, so updates require If-Match. Orders lock stock rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE, always in product I D order, so deadlocks are designed out.
Authentication is our own JWT issuer. Access tokens last fifteen minutes. Refresh tokens are hashed, rotate on every use, and reusing one revokes the whole token family.
Authorization is deny by default, with four named policies. A customer asking for someone else's data gets a 404, not a 403, so nothing leaks. Three rate limit policies protect the sensitive routes.

Only products are cached, with HybridCache and Valkey, and a Valkey outage never causes an error. Each dependency has exactly one retry layer, the database has a circuit breaker, and OpenTelemetry traces the whole path.
Now the BFF. I compared three options. Next dot J S as the backend. A plain single page app that holds tokens. Or a thin ASP.NET Core BFF.
The BFF won for one reason: tokens never reach the browser. It also gives one origin, so no CORS, no Node server in production, and the same dot net pipeline as the API.

On sign in, the BFF calls the API and stores the tokens in a Valkey session, encrypted with Data Protection. The browser gets one cookie. It is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite Strict, and uses the double underscore Host prefix.
So even if a script were injected into the page, there is no token for it to steal. Admin sessions also end after thirty minutes of inactivity.

Here is the trickiest part. The API treats a second use of a refresh token as theft. If a page fires twenty requests while the token is expiring, a naive client triggers a refresh storm, and signs the user out.

The BFF solves it with a single flight refresh coordinator. One refresh runs per session, and every other request awaits the same task. A test proves that twenty parallel requests cause exactly one refresh call.
The proxy is YARP with an explicit allow list. Unknown paths return 404. Login and refresh are never proxied. The BFF strips the browser's cookie, and adds the bearer token on the way through.

Every state changing request needs a custom X CSRF header and a matching Origin. A strict content security policy blocks inline scripts, rate limits apply per I P at the edge, and one trace I D flows from the BFF into the API.
The front end is Vite and React nineteen with the React Compiler, so there is no manual memoization. TypeScript runs in strict mode, and React Router loads routes lazily.
Server state lives in TanStack Query. Forms use React Hook Form with Zod. Styling is Tailwind four, with accessible Radix primitives through shadcn.

Code is organized by feature, and lint rules stop one feature importing another's internals. The Admin area is its own lazy chunk. The customer bundle is about one hundred sixty kilobytes gzipped, under a two hundred kilobyte budget that the pipeline enforces.
API types are generated from the committed OpenAPI document, and the pipeline fails if they drift. So a backend change that breaks the front end is caught at build time, not in production.
Errors arrive as ProblemDetails with a trace I D, and a slug maps to a plain message in the UI. Product edits send the entity tag back as If-Match, so the API can reject stale updates.

And here it is working: the catalog, an order placed, the account deletion flow, the admin dashboard, and product management. All against the real API, with demo data. There is a separate walkthrough video if you want every click.

Quality is layered. The BFF has ninety seven tests. The React app has two hundred thirty two, plus forty end to end Playwright tests with accessibility scans. The API has unit tests, integration tests on real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers, and architecture tests.

Azure Pipelines enforces it: an API freeze check, type checks, lint with zero warnings, bundle budgets, dependency audits, license checks, and Docker builds. The security reviews of the BFF and the front end are written up in the repo.

What does this mean for you as a client? AI assisted development gets features built fast. But every decision is documented, every rule is tested, and every change is reviewed. You get speed, without a codebase nobody understands.

To be clear, this is a proof of concept, built to show the approach. It lives on a feature branch and will be merged to main after final review. The Admin screens for orders, reports, and audit logs come next. If you want this level of rigor on your product, let's talk. Thanks for watching.
